title: Sizes of particles and their properties

notes.definition: Nanoscience is the study of structures that are 1 to 100 nm in size, roughly a few hundred atoms across (1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m). Nanoparticles have a very high surface area to volume ratio, so they can have different properties from the same material in bulk.
explanation: Particles are classified by size. Nanoparticles are between 1 nm and 100 nm across, where 1 nanometre (nm) is 1 × 10⁻⁹ m, one billionth of a metre. Structures this size contain of the order of a few hundred atoms. Fine particles, labelled PM2.5, have diameters between 100 nm and 2500 nm (1 × 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m), so nanoparticles are smaller than fine particles. Coarse particles, labelled PM10, have diameters between 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m and 1 × 10⁻⁵ m (2500 nm to 10 000 nm). Coarse particles are often referred to as dust.

You should be able to compare nanoparticle sizes with atoms and molecules. An atom has a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m), and small molecules are typically less than 1 nm across. A nanoparticle of 10 nm is therefore about 100 times wider than an atom's radius and contains hundreds of atoms. This is why nanoparticles sit between the size of atoms and molecules and the size of ordinary bulk materials.

The surface area to volume ratio (SA : V) is found by dividing surface area by volume. For a cube of side L, the surface area is 6L² (six square faces) and the volume is L³, so SA : V = 6L² ÷ L³ = 6 ÷ L. This shows that as the side of a cube decreases by a factor of 10, the surface area to volume ratio increases by a factor of 10. For example, a cube of side 10 nm has SA : V = 0.6 per nm, while a cube of side 1 nm has SA : V = 6 per nm.

Because nanoparticles are so small, they have a very high surface area to volume ratio. A much larger fraction of their atoms are at the surface, where they can react or interact with other substances. As a result, nanoparticles may have properties that are different from those of the same material in bulk (in large pieces). For example, a substance that is unreactive in bulk may become a useful catalyst as nanoparticles, and a white powder in bulk may be transparent as nanoparticles.

The high surface area to volume ratio also means that smaller quantities of a nanoparticulate material may be needed to be effective than for materials with normal particle sizes. For a catalyst, for example, reactions happen at the surface, so the same mass of catalyst spread into nanoparticles provides far more active surface. This can save money and resources.
keyFacts: Nanoparticles are 1 to 100 nm in size, of the order of a few hundred atoms.
Fine particles (PM2.5) are 100 to 2500 nm (1 × 10⁻⁷ m to 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m).
Coarse particles (PM10) are 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m to 1 × 10⁻⁵ m and are often called dust.
Atoms have a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m).
For a cube of side L: surface area = 6L², volume = L³, SA : V = 6 ÷ L.
When the side of a cube decreases by a factor of 10, SA : V increases by a factor of 10.
Nanoparticles may have different properties from bulk material because of their high SA : V.
Smaller quantities of nanoparticles may be needed to be effective.

keyTerms.definition: A unit of length equal to 1 × 10⁻⁹ m.
The study of structures that are 1 to 100 nm in size.
A particle between 1 nm and 100 nm in size, containing a few hundred atoms.
Particles with diameters between 100 nm and 2500 nm (1 × 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m).
Particles with diameters between 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m and 1 × 10⁻⁵ m, often called dust.
Surface area divided by volume; it increases as particles get smaller.
A material in large pieces with normal particle sizes, rather than as nanoparticles.

equations.name: Surface area to volume ratio
equations.formula: surface area to volume ratio = surface area ÷ volume
equations.units: per unit length, e.g. /nm or nm⁻¹

workedExamples.title: SA : V for two cubes
workedExamples.question: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 20 nm, and of a cube with sides of 2 nm. By what factor does the ratio change?
steps: Cube of side 20 nm: SA = 6 × 20² = 2400 nm²; V = 20³ = 8000 nm³; SA : V = 2400 ÷ 8000 = 0.3 per nm.
Cube of side 2 nm: SA = 6 × 2² = 24 nm²; V = 2³ = 8 nm³; SA : V = 24 ÷ 8 = 3 per nm.
workedExamples.answer: 0.3 per nm and 3 per nm: the side decreased by a factor of 10 and SA : V increased by a factor of 10.

workedExamples.question: A nanoparticle has a diameter of 40 nm. Write this in metres in standard form.

workedExamples.title: Classifying a particle
workedExamples.question: A particle in exhaust fumes has a diameter of 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ m. Is it a nanoparticle, a fine particle or a coarse particle?
steps: Convert to nm: 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ m ÷ 1 × 10⁻⁹ m = 1500 nm.

diagrams.title: Surface area to volume ratio
diagrams.caption: Dividing the side length of a cube by 10 multiplies its surface area to volume ratio by 10. Nanoparticles, being tiny, have very large surface area to volume ratios.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a smaller particle has a smaller surface area to volume ratio.
misconceptions.right: In fact smaller particles have a larger surface area to volume ratio. For a cube, SA : V = 6 ÷ L, so it increases as L decreases.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think nanoparticles are single atoms or molecules.
misconceptions.right: In fact nanoparticles are 1 to 100 nm across and contain of the order of a few hundred atoms; an atom has a radius of only about 0.1 nm.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think nanoparticles of a substance have exactly the same properties as the bulk material.
misconceptions.right: In fact their high surface area to volume ratio can give them different properties, such as greater reactivity or being transparent.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often mix up PM2.5 and PM10, thinking PM2.5 particles are larger.
misconceptions.right: In fact PM2.5 (fine) particles are smaller, up to 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m; PM10 (coarse) particles are larger, from 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m up to 1 × 10⁻⁵ m.

realWorld: Air-quality reports measure PM2.5 and PM10 levels because these particles from vehicle exhausts and dust can be breathed into the lungs.
Nanoparticles of catalysts such as platinum are used in car catalytic converters research, so that less of the expensive metal is needed for the same surface area.
Titanium dioxide is a white powder in bulk, but as nanoparticles it is transparent, which is why it can be used in clear sun creams.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Chemistry (8462) only, not Combined Science.
Nanoparticles are 1 to 100 nm (1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m); fine particles PM2.5 are 100 to 2500 nm; coarse particles PM10 are 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m to 1 × 10⁻⁵ m (dust).
As the side of a cube decreases by a factor of 10, the surface area to volume ratio increases by a factor of 10.
Nanoparticles may have different properties from bulk material because of their high surface area to volume ratio, and smaller quantities may be needed to be effective.
Compare nano dimensions with atoms (radius about 0.1 nm) and molecules.
examTips: Learn the size boundaries in both nm and metres: 1 to 100 nm, 100 to 2500 nm, and 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m to 1 × 10⁻⁵ m.
For SA : V of a cube, write out SA = 6L² and V = L³ before dividing; examiners award method marks.
To convert nm to m, multiply by 10⁻⁹; to convert m to nm, divide by 10⁻⁹ (multiply by 10⁹).
When explaining different properties of nanoparticles, always mention 'high surface area to volume ratio'.
If asked about the change in SA : V, use the factor: side ÷ 10 means SA : V × 10.
summary: Nanoparticles are 1 to 100 nm across; 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m.
Fine particles (PM2.5) are 100 to 2500 nm; coarse particles (PM10) are 2500 to 10 000 nm.
Atoms have a radius of about 0.1 nm, much smaller than nanoparticles.
For a cube, SA : V = 6 ÷ L.
Side decreases by 10 times, SA : V increases by 10 times.
High SA : V gives nanoparticles different properties and means less material is needed.

questions.question: What is the size range of nanoparticles?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1 to 100 nm
questions.explanation: Nanoparticles are 1 to 100 nm. 100 to 2500 nm is fine particles (PM2.5) and 2500 to 10 000 nm is coarse particles (PM10).

questions.question: What is 1 nanometre in metres?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1 × 10⁻⁹ m
questions.explanation: Nano means one billionth, so 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m. 10⁻⁶ m is a micrometre and 10⁻³ m is a millimetre.

questions.question: Which type of particle is often referred to as dust?
markScheme: 1 mark: Coarse particles (PM10)
questions.explanation: Coarse particles (PM10), 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m to 1 × 10⁻⁵ m in diameter, are often called dust.

questions.question: What happens to the surface area to volume ratio of a cube as its sides get smaller?
markScheme: 1 mark: It increases
questions.explanation: SA : V = 6 ÷ L for a cube, so a smaller L gives a larger ratio.

questions.question: Which particle diameter is a fine particle (PM2.5)?
markScheme: 1 mark: 5 × 10⁻⁷ m
questions.explanation: 5 × 10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm, which is in the 100 to 2500 nm range. 5 nm and 50 nm are nanoparticles; 5 × 10⁻⁶ m = 5000 nm is a coarse particle.

questions.question: The side of a cube is decreased from 50 nm to 5 nm. What happens to its surface area to volume ratio?
options: It decreases by a factor of 10
It increases by a factor of 10
It increases by a factor of 100
It increases by a factor of 1000
markScheme: 1 mark: It increases by a factor of 10
questions.explanation: When the side decreases by a factor of 10, SA : V increases by a factor of 10 (6 ÷ 50 = 0.12 to 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2).

questions.question: Why might nanoparticles of a substance have different properties from the same substance in bulk?
options: They are made of different atoms
They have a very high surface area to volume ratio
markScheme: 1 mark: They have a very high surface area to volume ratio
questions.explanation: The atoms are the same, but a much larger proportion of them are at the surface, so nanoparticles can behave differently.

questions.question: Approximately how many atoms does a nanoscale structure contain?
options: Of the order of a few hundred
markScheme: 1 mark: Of the order of a few hundred
questions.explanation: AQA describes nanoscale structures (1 to 100 nm) as being of the order of a few hundred atoms.

questions.question: An atom has a radius of about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. A nanoparticle has a diameter of 1 × 10⁻⁸ m. How many times larger is the nanoparticle's diameter than the atom's radius?
markScheme: 1 mark: 100
questions.explanation: 1 × 10⁻⁸ ÷ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 10². Subtracting the powers: −8 − (−10) = 2.

questions.question: Which list puts the particles in order of increasing size?
options: Coarse particle, fine particle, nanoparticle, atom
Atom, fine particle, nanoparticle, coarse particle
Atom, nanoparticle, fine particle, coarse particle
Nanoparticle, atom, fine particle, coarse particle
markScheme: 1 mark: Atom, nanoparticle, fine particle, coarse particle
questions.explanation: Atom (about 0.1 nm radius) < nanoparticle (1 to 100 nm) < fine particle (100 to 2500 nm) < coarse particle (2500 to 10 000 nm).

questions.question: What does PM10 refer to?
markScheme: 1 mark: Coarse particles
questions.explanation: PM10 refers to coarse particles with diameters up to 1 × 10⁻⁵ m (10 micrometres).

questions.question: Calculate the surface area of a cube with sides of 10 nm.
markScheme: 1 mark: 6 × 10² = 600 nm²
questions.explanation: A cube has six square faces, each 10 × 10 = 100 nm². 6 × 100 = 600 nm².

questions.question: Calculate the volume of a cube with sides of 10 nm.
markScheme: 1 mark: 10³ = 1000 nm³
questions.explanation: Volume = side × side × side = 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 nm³.

questions.question: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 5 nm.
markScheme: 1 mark: SA = 6 × 5² = 150 nm² and V = 5³ = 125 nm³
1 mark: 150 ÷ 125 = 1.2 per nm
questions.explanation: SA : V = 150 ÷ 125 = 1.2 per nm. You can check with 6 ÷ L = 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2.

questions.question: A nanoparticle has a diameter of 50 nm. Write this diameter in metres. Give your answer in standard form.
questions.explanation: Multiply by 10⁻⁹: 50 × 10⁻⁹ m = 5 × 10⁻⁸ m.

questions.question: The upper limit for fine particles (PM2.5) is 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m. Convert this to nanometres.
questions.explanation: Divide by 10⁻⁹ (multiply by 10⁹): 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁹ = 2.5 × 10³ = 2500 nm.

questions.question: The side length of a cube is reduced from 100 nm to 1 nm. By what factor does its surface area to volume ratio increase?
markScheme: 1 mark: SA : V goes from 6 ÷ 100 = 0.06 to 6 ÷ 1 = 6 per nm
questions.explanation: The side decreases by a factor of 100, so SA : V increases by a factor of 100. Each factor of 10 decrease in side gives a factor of 10 increase in SA : V.

questions.question: A sugar cube has sides of 1 cm. It is cut into small cubes with sides of 1 mm. Calculate the total surface area of all the small cubes in cm². (1 cm = 10 mm)
markScheme: 1 mark: number of small cubes = 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000, each with SA = 6 mm²
1 mark: total = 6000 mm² = 60 cm²
questions.explanation: The original cube has SA = 6 cm². After cutting, 1000 cubes × 6 mm² = 6000 mm²; since 1 cm² = 100 mm², this is 60 cm², 10 times larger. Same volume, 10 times the surface.

questions.question: An atom has a radius of 0.1 nm. Calculate how many times larger the diameter of a 30 nm nanoparticle is than the diameter of the atom.
markScheme: 1 mark: diameter of atom = 0.2 nm
questions.explanation: Compare like with like: diameter with diameter. The atom's diameter is 2 × 0.1 = 0.2 nm, so 30 ÷ 0.2 = 150. Using the radius gives 300, which is wrong.

questions.question: A fine particle has a diameter of 2000 nm and a nanoparticle has a diameter of 50 nm. How many times larger is the diameter of the fine particle?
questions.explanation: Both are in nm, so divide directly: 2000 ÷ 50 = 40.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term nanoscience.
acceptedAnswers: study of structures 1 to 100 nm in size
very small structures of a few hundred atoms
markScheme: 1 mark: the study of structures that are 1 to 100 nm in size
questions.explanation: Nanoscience refers to structures 1 to 100 nm across, of the order of a few hundred atoms.

questions.question: Explain why nanoparticles may have different properties from the same material in bulk.
acceptedAnswers: high surface area to volume ratio
markScheme: 1 mark: nanoparticles have a (very) high surface area to volume ratio
1 mark: so a much larger proportion of their atoms are at the surface (able to react or interact)
questions.explanation: The key phrase is high surface area to volume ratio, linked to more atoms being exposed at the surface.

questions.question: Explain why smaller quantities of a nanoparticle catalyst may be needed than of a catalyst with normal particle sizes.
acceptedAnswers: high surface area to volume ratio
markScheme: 1 mark: nanoparticles have a high surface area to volume ratio
1 mark: so a small mass provides a large surface area where reactions can occur
questions.explanation: Catalysts work at their surface, so more surface per gram means less catalyst is needed for the same effect.

questions.question: Give the diameter ranges, in nm, of fine particles (PM2.5) and of nanoparticles.
markScheme: 1 mark: fine particles: 100 to 2500 nm
1 mark: nanoparticles: 1 to 100 nm
questions.explanation: Learn the boundaries: nanoparticles 1 to 100 nm, fine particles 100 to 2500 nm, coarse particles 2500 to 10 000 nm.

questions.question: A cube of a metal has sides of 1 × 10⁻⁷ m. Determine whether it is a nanoparticle and calculate its surface area to volume ratio in nm⁻¹.
markScheme: 1 mark: 1 × 10⁻⁷ m = 100 nm
1 mark: this is at the upper limit of the nanoparticle range (1 to 100 nm) / boundary with fine particles
1 mark: SA : V = 6 ÷ 100 = 0.06 nm⁻¹
questions.explanation: Convert first: 1 × 10⁻⁷ ÷ 10⁻⁹ = 100 nm, the boundary between nanoparticles and fine particles. SA : V = 6L² ÷ L³ = 6 ÷ 100 = 0.06 per nm.

questions.question: Name the type of particle that has a diameter between 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m and 1 × 10⁻⁵ m.
markScheme: 1 mark: coarse particles (PM10) / dust
questions.explanation: Coarse particles (PM10) have diameters from 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m to 1 × 10⁻⁵ m and are often called dust.

questions.question: For a cube, surface area to volume ratio = 6 ÷ L, where L is the side length. Describe what happens to the surface area to volume ratio when the side length is halved, and explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: the ratio doubles (increases by a factor of 2)
1 mark: because the ratio is 6 ÷ L, so it is inversely proportional to L / surface area falls by 4 but volume falls by 8
questions.explanation: Halving L gives 6 ÷ (L/2) = 12 ÷ L, twice the original. Area scales with L² and volume with L³, so volume falls faster than surface area.

questions.question: Compare nanoparticles, fine particles and coarse particles in terms of their sizes. Include sizes in both nanometres and metres.
markScheme: Indicative content: nanoparticles 1 to 100 nm (1 × 10⁻⁹ m to 1 × 10⁻⁷ m); contain a few hundred atoms; fine particles PM2.5: 100 to 2500 nm (1 × 10⁻⁷ m to 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m); coarse particles PM10: 2500 to 10 000 nm (2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m to 1 × 10⁻⁵ m); often called dust; nanoparticles are the smallest; atoms (radius about 0.1 nm) are smaller still; 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct size ranges for all three types in both units, with a clear comparison of their relative sizes.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct size ranges or an order of size with little numerical detail.
questions.explanation: Top answers give correct ranges in both nm and metres and clearly state which is largest and smallest.

questions.question:
A student has a cube of silver with sides of 1 cm and an equal mass of silver as nanoparticles.
Use ideas about surface area to volume ratio to explain why the silver nanoparticles may behave differently from the cube. Include calculations to support your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: SA : V of a cube = 6 ÷ L; for the 1 cm cube: SA = 6 cm², V = 1 cm³, SA : V = 6 per cm; for a nanoparticle cube of side 10 nm: SA = 600 nm², V = 1000 nm³, SA : V = 0.6 per nm; convert 1 cm = 1 × 10⁷ nm so the cube's SA : V = 6 × 10⁻⁷ per nm; the nanoparticles have a SA : V about 10⁶ times greater; each factor of 10 decrease in side increases SA : V by a factor of 10; much larger total surface area for the same mass; a far greater proportion of silver atoms are at the surface; so nanoparticles may be more reactive or have different properties (for example antibacterial action, catalytic activity, different colour); smaller quantities needed to be effective.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct calculations of SA : V for both, a valid numerical comparison, and a clear explanation linking high SA : V to different properties and smaller quantities needed.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some correct calculation and a link between surface area to volume ratio and properties, but the comparison is incomplete or contains errors.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that nanoparticles have a larger surface area or are more reactive, with little or no calculation.
questions.explanation: The strongest answers calculate SA : V for both sizes, compare them in the same units, and explain that more surface atoms means different behaviour and that less material is needed.
